title: Bias is a Math Problem, AI Bias is a Technical Problem: 10-year Literature Review of AI/LLM Bias Research Reveals Narrow [Gender-Centric] Conceptions of ‘Bias’, and Academia-Industry Gap
relevance_assessment: Highly relevant – the paper systematically reviews AI/LLM bias literature over the past decade, directly addressing methods, findings, and limitations of bias research in LLMs, which aligns with the requested analysis of AI LLM bias trends.
key_findings: 82% (155/189) of surveyed papers did not define “bias”, relying on implicit or purely mathematical definitions (Abstract; §4.1).
79.9% (151/189) of papers focused on gender bias, especially gender‑occupation associations; other axes (race/ethnicity, age, religion, nationality) were far less represented (Abstract; §4.2).
Only 10.6% (20/189) of papers offered actionable implementation recommendations for real‑world systems, highlighting a substantial academia‑industry “last‑mile” gap (Abstract; §4.3).
When definitions were provided, many framed bias as inherently negative; a minority noted that bias can be neutral or even beneficial, cautioning against equating bias with harm (§4.1).
Binary gender constructions dominate; 138 of the gender‑bias papers used binary categories, with 114 explicitly noting this as a limitation (§4.2).
A few studies expanded beyond Western contexts (e.g., caste bias in India, dialect bias in Arabic/German, bias against stutterers), but these are outliers (§4.2).
limitations: Corpus limited to four premier venues (*ACL, FAccT, NeurIPS, AAAI) and to papers passing title/abstract screening; relevant work in other venues (e.g., CHI) or on arXiv may be omitted (§7).
Reliance on keyword search ("bias" OR "harm" OR "stereotype") may miss papers that discuss bias using different terminology (§7).
Binary gender focus reflects dataset availability rather than intentional design, limiting applicability to non‑binary or intersectional identities (§4.2).
The review does not evaluate the actual effectiveness of the debiasing methods reported; it only notes their presence (§4.3).
Implementation recommendations are sparse, and the paper does not assess barriers such as venue page limits or industry confidentiality that may cause this gap (§4.3).
evidence_snippets: “82% (155/189) papers did not provide a definition of ‘bias’, opting instead to simply state that biases and stereotypes exist… 94 of these 155 papers have been published in the past 5 years…" (Abstract).

“79.9% (151/189) papers focus on gender bias (mostly gender and occupation bias)… race/ethnicity (30.2%; 57/189), age (20.6%; 39/189), religion (19.1%; 36/189), nationality (13.2%; 25/189)" (Abstract).
“Only 10.6% (20/189) include recommendations for how to implement their findings or contributions in real‑world AI systems… This indicates a concerning academia‑industry gap” (Abstract).
“Within the remaining 94/155 papers, ‘bias’ is either evaluated or defined purely mathematically…" (§4.1).
“When bias is defined, researchers often attach a negative sentiment… examples: ‘Social bias can be defined as the manifestation…’ ” (§4.1).

“138 consider exclusively binary constructions of gender and 114 of these mention such a binary focus as a limitation… ‘Due to practical reasons and existing lack of datasets, we limited our research to only the binary genders.’” (§4.2).
“89.4% (169/189) papers do not include ways to operationalize their proposed mitigation strategies…” (§4.3).
“The search did not cover the CHI Conference… only 6 of 313 CHI papers would have passed manual screening, so relevant papers may have been missed.” (§7).
summary: The review of 189 papers from top AI/LLM venues shows that most bias research lacks a clear conceptual definition of bias, treating it as a purely technical issue to be eliminated. Gender bias dominates the field, with nearly 80% of studies focusing on binary gender‑occupation stereotypes, while other identity axes receive far less attention. Only a tiny fraction of work (≈10%) provides practical guidance for deploying debiasing methods in real‑world systems, revealing a pronounced academia‑industry gap. The authors note methodological limits, such as venue‑centric sampling, keyword‑driven screening, and binary gender assumptions driven by dataset availability. These findings call for broader, more inclusive definitions of bias, expanded study of under‑represented populations, and stronger emphasis on implementation pathways to bridge research and practice in AI/LLM fairness.
